metadata.title: An integrated approach for detecting and classifying pores and surface topology for fatigue assessment 316L manufactured by powder bed fusion of metals using a laser beam using  µCT and machine learning algorithms - Data
metadata.description:
Description: This dataset contains micro-computed tomography (µCT) scans and fatigue test data for specimens manufactured from 316L stainless steel using laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M). All specimens were scanned by µCT and subsequently subjected to fatigue testing. The dataset links the fatigue test results of each specimen to the corresponding µCT scan, enabling the investigation of relationships between internal manufacturing defects, specimen characteristics, and fatigue performance. The specimen geometry, manufacturing conditions, experimental procedures, and evaluation methods are described in the related journal publication.

Related Journal publication: Diller J, Siebert L, Winkler M, et al. An integrated approach for detecting and classifying pores and surface topology for fatigue assessment 316L manufactured by powder bed fusion of metals using a laser beam using μCT and machine learning algorithms. Fatigue Fract Eng Mater Struct. 2024;47(9):3392-3407. doi:10.1111/ffe.14375

metadata.title: Peculiarities of the psychoemotional state of pregnant women with congenital heart diseases
metadata.description:
Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a pathology which is characterized by heart structure malformations. Pregnant women with CHD require the medical help of a doctor’s multidisciplinary team before, during and after pregnancy. The number of pregnant women with CHD has increased over the past decades. Stress is an integral part of the present time, and people with CHD have a higher risk of emotional, behavioral and social problems. Current results indicate the need for a holistic approach focused on pregnant women with CHD during the whole pregnancy.
The objective: to analyze the psychoemotional state of pregnant women with CHD.
Materials and methods. 180 pregnant women with CHD were examined. The main group (MG) – 150 women: subgroup A –
30 pregnant women with unoperated heart defects and heart failure (HF) II–III functional class (FC) of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) and pulmonary hypertension, subgroup B – 60 pregnant women with operated CHD and HF II–III FC, subgroup C – 60 pregnant women with unoperated heart defects and HF I FC. Control group (CG) – 30 women with a physiological course of pregnancy without cardiac pathology. For psychological testing the observation, conversation, interview and methods for determination of the levels of depression (PHQ-9 test), anxiety (Spilberger test) and the formation of emotional attachment between mother and fetus. Statistical processing of results and graphic design were carried out using Microsoft Excel 2016 and Statistica 10 for Windows.
Results. 74% of women (n = 37) in subgroup B had low mood and tearfulness, which can mostly be explained by a long stay in the hospital. Women in the CG were characterized by an increased level of reactive anxiety with a normal level of personal anxiety. In subgroup A 100% of pregnant women had a fear of death during childbirth or after childbirth. 33.3% (n = 10) of women in this subgroup practically did not make plans for the future, 66.7% (n = 20) of pregnant women were confident that everything will be fine, but constantly hoped for help from the partners. 18% (n = 27) of women in the MG had increased depression indicators according to the PHQ-9 test, and 22% (n = 33) of pregnant women in this group had borderline values. Having analyzed the pictures of women, we can conclude that there are common features in all the results: anxiety, self-doubt, conflict.
Conclusions. The psycho-emotional state of pregnant women with CHD requires both medical and psychological support. In this regard, there is an urgent need to develop a program of psychological support and comprehensive preparation for childbirth for women with this pathology.

metadata.title: Congenital Heart Diseases: Explaining Shunts and the Fallot Complex
metadata.description:
• Congenital Heart Diseases: Explaining Shunts and the Fallot Complex 

Author: Abhinav Kumar Sharma Hrishikesh Rathod and Kartikay Dhillon

Under the Guidance of Abdiraimov Isakender sir

Abstract

Background: Congenital heart diseases (CHDs) are the most common type of birth defect, and critical types of them present during the neonatal period or infancy. It is important for medical students across all specialties to be familiar with the embryology, pathophysiology, and clinical significance of common CHDs.

Objective: This is a broad overview of the three general categories of CHDs: left-to-right shunts (Atrial and Ventricular Septal Defects) and the complex cyanotic lesion, Tetralogy of Fallot. It attempts to bridge foundational knowledge with clinical practice, highlighting the "why" of the physical exam findings and management strategies.

Key Insights: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) and Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) are acyanotic defects that initially create left-to-right shunts, leading to right heart volume overload and secondary pulmonary hypertension. In contrast, Tetralogy of Fallot is cyanotic with a right-to-left shunt due to right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Its clinical course is characterized by hypercyanotic "tet" spells. Management ranges from observation in small ASDs to percutaneous or surgical closure of large defects and VSDs, to infant corrective surgery for Tetralogy of Fallot.

This knowledge of the classic CHD models allows the student to think through any complex heart defect by taking into account the shunting direction, the effects on hemodynamics, and the pressure/resistance relationship. Early recognition and intervention are paramount to preventing chronic complications like Eisenmenger's syndrome and ensuring survival to adulthood.

1. Introduction

Congenital heart diseases are a consequence of cardiac embryogenesis mistakes, more precisely between weeks 3-8 of pregnancy. They are present in roughly 1% of live births and contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality in children. For students of medicine, pathophysiologic classification of CHDs—i.e., whether there is or is not cyanosis and the direction of the shunt—is a most helpful organizing principle. The most common acyanotic shunts (ASD, VSD) and the ubiquitous cyanotic defect, Tetralogy of Fallot, and its variants will be addressed in this article.

2. Embryological Basis

The heart develops from two endocardial tubes coming together to create a primitive heart tube, which then undergoes looping and septation. Key structures for our interests:

· Atrial Septum: Formed by the septum primum and septum secundum to create the foramen ovale.

· Ventricular Septum: A muscular part develops up from the apex, and a membranous part closes the final gap. VSDs most commonly occur in the membranous septum.

· Conotruncal Septum: Divides the primitive truncus arteriosus into pulmonary artery and aorta. Abnormal development of the conotruncus provides the basis for Tetralogy of Fallot.

3. Acyanotic Congenital Heart Diseases: Left-to-Right Shunts

These defects allow oxygenated blood to shunt from systemic (left) to pulmonary (right) circulation, resulting in increased pulmonary flow without initial cyanosis. The most significant long-term complication is the onset of pulmonary hypertension.

3.1. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)

An ASD is an interatrial communication. The Ostium Secundum ASD (70%) is the most frequent and occurs in the region of the fossa ovalis.

Pathophysiology:

· After birth, left atrial pressure (8-10 mmHg) is higher than that of the right atrium (3-5 mmHg), and thus there is a left-to-right shunt.

· It leads to volume overload of the right atrium and right ventricle, both of which become enlarged.

· Increased pulmonary blood flow, but normally low pulmonary vascular resistance for decades.

Clinical Features:

· Most often asymptomatic in children. Dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, palpitations may arise in adults.

· Auscultation: A fixed and wide S2 splitting is the typical finding. A low-pitched mid-systolic (ejection) murmur is heard over the pulmonary area due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve.

· Complications: Right heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, and, if untreated, Eisenmenger's syndrome (shunt reversal to right-to-left).

Management:

· Small defects may close spontaneously. Larger defects or those causing right heart dilation must be closed, either percutaneously with a device or surgically.

3.2. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

A VSD is a communication between the ventricles. The most common type is the Perimembranous VSD (80%), in the membranous septum near the aortic valve.

Pathophysiology:

· During systole, high-pressure left ventricular blood is shunted to the right ventricle and into pulmonary circulation.

· Right ventricle volume and pressure overloading and severe left atrial and ventricular volume overloading (as the blood gets returned on the left side via the lungs).

· The shunt size will depend on the defect size and pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance ratio (PVR/SVR).

Clinical Features:

· Presentation is size-dependent. Large VSDs present with heart failure in infancy: tachypnea, poor feeding, repeated pulmonary infections, and failure to thrive.

· Auscultation: Harsh, loud holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border. In the event of a large shunt, mitral diastolic rumble can be heard at the apex.

· Complications: Congestive heart failure, infective endocarditis, and Eisenmenger's syndrome.

Management:

· Small muscular VSDs close spontaneously. Large symptomatic VSDs must be surgically repaired, typically in the initial year of life to prevent pulmonary vascular disease.

4. Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease: Tetralogy of Fallot

The most common cyanotic CHD after infancy is Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). It is due to a solitary embryological defect: anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular septum. This results in four characteristic features, recalled using the mnemonic PROV:

1. Pulmonary Stenosis (Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction): Most significant abnormality deciding severity.

2. Right Ventricular Hypertrophy: Secondary to the pressure overload due to pulmonary stenosis.

3. Overriding Aorta: The aorta overrides the VSD and receives blood supply from both ventricles.

4. Ventricular Septal Defect: Usually a large, non-restrictive defect.

4.1. Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation

The clinical presentation is overshadowed by the severity of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO).

· Right-to-Left Shunt: The obstructed pulmonary stenosis leads to increased right ventricular pressure. When RV pressure is greater than LV pressure, deoxygenated blood is shunted from the VSD into the aorta, causing cyanosis.

· Hypercyanotic Spells ("Tet Spells"): Acute, potentially life-threatening spells of cyanosis and dyspnea. Triggers are crying, defecation, or feeding. The pathophysiology is sudden increase in RVOTO (infundibular spasm) and/or decrease in SVR, increasing the right-to-left shunting.

· Physical Exam:

  · Cyanosis and Clubbing (older, unrepaired children).

  · Auscultation: A harsh systolic ejection murmur (crescendo-decrescendo) due to pulmonary stenosis. Significantly, the VSD itself is silent because it is large and non-restrictive (no pressure gradient). During a tet spell, the murmur may become softer or disappear because less blood runs through the stenotic valve.

4.2. Variants: Triad and Pentad of Fallot

· Triad of Fallot: Variant which comprises Pulmonary Stenosis, Right Ventricular Hypertrophy, and an Atrial Septal Defect (or Patent Foramen Ovale). It shares the same pathophysiology as TOF but with an atrial-level shunt.

· Pentad of Fallot: Refers to the classical tetrad with an Atrial Septal Defect or Patent Foramen Ovale.

4.3. Treatment

· Medical: Propranolol or atenolol to prevent tet spells by blocking infundibular spasm.

· Surgical: Cured with definitive repair, typically performed in the first few months of life. It involves 1) VSD closure and 2) RVOTO relief (resection of obstructive muscle and pulmonary valve patching, if necessary).

5. Diagnostic Tools

1. Chest X-Ray (CXR):

   · ASD/VSD: Cardiomegaly, dilated pulmonary arteries, increased pulmonary vascular markings.

· TOF: "Boot-shaped heart" (coeur en sabot) due to RVH and an inverted apex, with oligemic (decreased) lung fields.

2. Electrocardiogram (ECG):

   · ASD: Right axis deviation, partial RBBB pattern (rSR' in V1).

   · VSD: Biventricular hypertrophy.

   · TOF: Right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy.

3. Echocardiography: Gold standard for diagnosis. Provides absolute anatomical and functional assessment, such as direction of the shunt and pressure gradients.

4. Cardiac Catheterization: Used in the event of complicated anatomy, to measure pulmonary pressures, or for therapeutic intervention (e.g., device closure of an atrial septal defect).

6. The Dire Complication: Eisenmenger's Syndrome

This is an obstructive condition that develops due to a long-standing left-to-right shunt (due to a large ASD, VSD, or PDA) resulting in extensive pulmonary vascular obstructive disease. Pulmonary hypertension that develops becomes greater than the systemic resistance, and the shunt is reversed to right-to-left. The patient develops cyanosis and has a poor long-term prognosis. It is a big reminder of the necessity of early intervention in CHD.

7. Conclusion

For the medical student, an understanding of ASD, VSD, and Tetralogy of Fallot forms a cornerstone of clinical cardiology. The distinction between acyanotic and cyanotic lesions relies on the direction of shunting, which in turn relies on the interdependence of pressures and resistances of the heart and pulmonary circulation. From the fixed-split S2 of ASD to the hypercyanotic spell of TOF, clinical presentation is a precise reflection of the hemodynamics. The appreciation of these principles allows a rational and effective management of any congenital heart lesion.
